cards.title: Fully dynamic single-source distances beyond rebuilding
cards.formal: Can single-source distances in a fully dynamic graph be maintained faster than recomputing them from scratch after every edge update, while keeping distance queries constant-time? This restores the case named by the selected 2017 source paragraph: both insertions and deletions are allowed. The passage does not fix a single quantitative accuracy-and-time target, and later algorithms already improve on rebuilding in important variants; the remaining formulation choices are recorded below.

source_formulation.text: That is, we do not know how to do better than reconstructing from scratch after every edge update.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

cards.why: Dynamic shortest paths asks how much computation can be reused as a network changes. Separating update cost, query cost, approximation and graph density is essential to deciding whether a data structure meaningfully improves on a static computation.
cards.status_note: Read the complete source paragraph and full author version, 2019 Problem 1.1 and Theorem 1.5, and 2023 Theorem 1.1 with their introductory qualifications. Searches through 12 September 2026 found later improvements incompatible with presenting the saved blanket limitation as current. The remaining accuracy, randomness, preprocessing and quantitative-saving choices prevent a single fully specified open proposition.

Its setting discusses both exact and approximate distances, while the saved sentence does not select the required approximation factor, randomness/adversary guarantees, amortized versus worst-case update cost, preprocessing bound, or a quantified saving and graph-density regime. The paper title cannot supply a deterministic-only restriction for this separate introductory observation. Later work already beats rebuilding for weighted approximate dense instances and exact unweighted dense instances, so the blanket 2017 “nothing better” statement is no longer a current open question. cards.definitions:
The surrounding source setting is an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with positive edge weights and a fixed source \(s\in V\). A shortest-path distance \(d_{G}(s,v)\) is the minimum total edge weight along a path from \(s\) to \(v\), with \(d_{G}(s,s)=0\) and distance \(+\infty\) for an unreachable vertex. Let \(n=|V|\) and let \(m\) denote the number of current edges when discussing a static baseline.

Fully dynamic maintenance allows arbitrary interleavings of edge insertions, deletions and weight changes in both directions. Updates arrive online. Decremental maintenance permits only deletions and increases; incremental maintenance permits only insertions and decreases. The deterministic algorithm proved in the 2017 paper is decremental, whereas the selected introductory limitation explicitly says fully dynamic.

A query supplies one vertex \(v\) and asks for its distance from the fixed source in the current graph. The source uses constant-time distance queries unless stated otherwise. Numerical distance reporting is separate from outputting the entire path or an entire source tree, whose output may contain many edges.

For approximation factor \(\alpha\geq1\), the source's convention is a one-sided estimate
\[d_{G}(s,v)\leq\widehat d(s,v)\leq\alpha\,d_{G}(s,v).\]
The case \(\alpha=1\) requires exact distances. The paper's positive decremental theorem uses \(\alpha=1+\varepsilon\). Unreachable vertices must be reported as unreachable, and the source distance remains zero. This convention does not by itself specify which accuracy is intended in the broad fully dynamic question.

Preprocessing is the initial construction cost. Worst-case update time bounds every individual update; amortized update time bounds the aggregate over a sequence after accounting for preprocessing. Fully dynamic sequences can reinsert deleted edges indefinitely, so their length is not bounded by the initial number of edges. A decremental total-update bound cannot be read as a fully dynamic per-update guarantee.

Rebuilding runs a static shortest-path algorithm after each update and stores the source distances for subsequent constant-time lookups. Under standard arithmetic assumptions, Dijkstra's algorithm takes \(O(m+n\log n)\) time. The source suppresses logarithmic factors when referring to its nearly linear rebuilding baseline. On dense graphs the cost is quadratic in \(n\); a subquadratic bound in \(n\) can improve this regime without being sublinear in \(m\) on sparse graphs.

A completed target must specify an accuracy, allowed randomization and success guarantee, adversary access to previous outputs, preprocessing cost, worst-case or amortized accounting, and the required saving as a function of graph size and density. It must also fix the weight representation and arithmetic costs. A positive-real-weight statement with unit-cost arithmetic differs from a bit-complexity claim for arbitrarily long encoded weights. The source sentence alone does not fix all these choices.
cards.answer_criterion: First fix an unresolved variant with explicit accuracy, computational model, query bound and asymptotic update target. An algorithm must meet all these guarantees for every allowed online sequence after the stated preprocessing. An impossibility result must state its assumptions. A faster algorithm only for unweighted, dense, planar or partially dynamic graphs is not automatically a solution for every weighted fully dynamic formulation.

context_blocks.title: The paper title describes a different result
context_blocks.text: The 2017 theorem gives a deterministic approximate decremental data structure for positive weighted undirected graphs. The saved sentence instead motivates work by discussing the harder fully dynamic setting; transferring the title to that sentence changed its subject.

context_blocks.title: Weighted approximation later beats rebuilding on dense graphs
context_blocks.text: Van den Brand and Nanongkai give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate data structure explicitly maintaining all source distances, with historical update bound \(\widetilde O(n^{1.823}\varepsilon^{-2}\log W)\) and preprocessing \(\widetilde O(n^{2.621}\varepsilon^{-1}\log W)\). Here weights lie in \([1,W]\); additional logarithmic factors in accuracy are suppressed. Their high-probability guarantee allows adaptive updates. Explicit storage gives constant-time distance lookups. This improves the quadratic dense-graph baseline, but is not a deterministic all-density sublinear-in-edges result.

context_blocks.title: Exact unweighted maintenance also improved
context_blocks.text: The 2023 theorem gives deterministic worst-case \(O(n^{1.969})\) update and single-source-query time on unweighted directed graphs. For a fixed source, computing and storing its distance vector after each update retains that update exponent and supplies constant-time lookups. The unweighted promise matters; the source separately discusses conditional barriers for sufficiently large polynomial integer weights.

context_blocks.title: The old blanket limitation is no longer the status
context_blocks.text: The later papers distinguish exact weighted, exact unweighted and approximate weighted maintenance, as well as preprocessing and density regimes. Their results show why the historical “nothing better than rebuilding” observation cannot be promoted to a current universal claim without choosing a precise remaining target.

cards.context:
The 2017 theorem gives a deterministic approximate decremental data structure for positive weighted undirected graphs. The saved sentence instead motivates work by discussing the harder fully dynamic setting; transferring the title to that sentence changed its subject.

Van den Brand and Nanongkai give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate data structure explicitly maintaining all source distances, with historical update bound \(\widetilde O(n^{1.823}\varepsilon^{-2}\log W)\) and preprocessing \(\widetilde O(n^{2.621}\varepsilon^{-1}\log W)\). Here weights lie in \([1,W]\); additional logarithmic factors in accuracy are suppressed. Their high-probability guarantee allows adaptive updates. Explicit storage gives constant-time distance lookups. This improves the quadratic dense-graph baseline, but is not a deterministic all-density sublinear-in-edges result.

The 2023 theorem gives deterministic worst-case \(O(n^{1.969})\) update and single-source-query time on unweighted directed graphs. For a fixed source, computing and storing its distance vector after each update retains that update exponent and supplies constant-time lookups. The unweighted promise matters; the source separately discusses conditional barriers for sufficiently large polynomial integer weights.

The later papers distinguish exact weighted, exact unweighted and approximate weighted maintenance, as well as preprocessing and density regimes. Their results show why the historical “nothing better than rebuilding” observation cannot be promoted to a current universal claim without choosing a precise remaining target.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
